unit.unitOverview: Collaboration is working with other people towards a shared goal, sharing the work fairly and helping each other, so that together you produce something better than any of you could alone. It is not just being in the same room. Real collaboration means agreeing a goal, dividing roles fairly, contributing useful ideas, listening and building on each other, handling disagreement with respect, and reviewing honestly how you worked.

explainers.title: Welcome back to Global Perspectives
explainers.body:
Welcome to Unit 5 of Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. By now you know that this subject is not about memorising facts. It teaches you a set of thinking and working skills that you can use for the rest of your life, in any subject and in the real world around you.

There are six skills in Global Perspectives, and you grow all of them over your years here:

This unit is all about the fifth skill: Collaboration. So far, most of your Global Perspectives work has been something you could do largely on your own: researching, analysing, evaluating and reflecting. Collaboration is different. You cannot collaborate by yourself. It is the skill of getting good things done with other people — agreeing a shared goal, sharing the work fairly, listening to each other, handling disagreements kindly, and finishing something together that no single person could have made alone.

You may wonder why this matters beyond school. Almost everything important in the adult world is built by teams. A new clinic is designed by doctors, builders and planners working together. A family wedding in Hargeisa is organised by many relatives sharing tasks. A small shop runs because the owner, the supplier and the staff cooperate. A borehole gets dug because a community agrees on it, funds it and works on it together. People who can collaborate well get chosen for the best work, and they get more done. That is why we practise it on purpose here.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — breaking a topic into parts and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how strong an argument or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you have changed your mind.
Collaboration — working well with other people towards a shared goal.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so others understand you.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit: a special split
explainers.body:
You are learning in Ehel Academy's self-paced way. Three kinds of support work together for you:

Collaboration needs one careful change to this model, and it is the most important idea in the whole unit. You cannot truly collaborate with a book, and you cannot truly collaborate alone. Real collaboration needs real people. So in this unit your learning splits neatly into two halves:

So all through this unit you will see the same rhythm: plan it with your AI tutor now, then carry it out with your group in your next teacher session. Think of your AI tutor as the practice ground and your teacher session as the real match. A footballer who trains hard alone plays far better in the real game. In the same way, a learner who rehearses teamwork with their tutor becomes a much stronger teammate when the real people are in the room.

Here is what that looks like in practice. Before a teacher session, you might tell your AI tutor: I think my group will argue about whether to make a poster or a video. You then ask it to help you prepare a calm way to suggest a compromise, and you practise saying the words. When the disagreement really happens in the session, you are ready and steady, because you planned on your own and now you perform together. That is the whole method of this unit in one example.
bullets: You, learning at your own pace. You read, think and prepare in your own time.
Your AI tutor, available 24 hours a day. It is your study partner and, in this unit, your planning and rehearsal partner.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you meet the other learners and work together face to face.

Plan and rehearse with your AI tutor. On your own time, you use your tutor to get ready. You plan the roles, practise active listening, rehearse how you will disagree politely, try out your ideas, and get feedback before anyone else hears them. Your tutor can even pretend to be a difficult teammate so you can practise safely.

Do the real collaboration with people. The actual teamwork happens in your twice-weekly teacher sessions, where you work face to face with your group, and at home, where you work with your family and community.

explainers.title: Meet the group we will follow this unit
explainers.body:
In the last unit you followed one learner. Because this unit is about teamwork, we will follow a whole group of Year 7 learners at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. They are an ordinary team, with ordinary strengths and ordinary disagreements, and you will see exactly how they work through each collaboration skill.

Notice that no one in this group is good at everything, and that is completely normal. A strong team is not made of five people who are all the same. It is made of different people whose strengths fit together, so that the team as a whole can do what no single member could. As you meet each skill, watch how this group uses each person's strength — and how they help Idris, their quietest member, to take part.

You will also watch them disagree, get stuck, and get a few things wrong along the way, because that is what real teams do. What makes them a good team is not that they never struggle. It is that they keep working together kindly, and honestly, until they get there. Your own team will be exactly the same, and that is nothing to worry about.
bullets: Nadia is organised. She likes making a plan, keeping track of who is doing what, and meeting deadlines.
Sami is full of ideas. He is creative and loves suggesting new ways to do things, though not all of his ideas work.
Layla is a calm listener. She notices when someone has gone quiet and gently brings them back into the conversation.
Rohan is confident speaking to a group. He is happy to stand up and present the team's work to the class.
Idris is thoughtful but shy. He often has good ideas but holds them back unless someone makes space for him.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: a shared group project
explainers.body:
This unit builds towards one ongoing project we call your Challenge. In the earlier units your Challenge was mostly yours alone. In this unit the Challenge becomes a shared outcome: something your whole group plans, builds and finishes together, such as a poster, a presentation, or a short video that raises awareness about a real problem.

Here are some global topics that are also very real in the Horn of Africa. Any of these could become your group's shared Challenge:

The group we follow chose plastic waste. They noticed that thin plastic bags from the Hargeisa market blow into the streets, block the drains, and cause flooding when the rains come, and that some bags reach the coast where they harm sea animals. Their shared outcome will be a poster and a short presentation for the rest of the school, urging people to switch to reusable cloth bags. You will watch them build it, skill by skill.

Your topic will probably be different, and that is good. Another group of learners at Ehel Academy in Mogadishu chose road safety near their school, and a third group chose keeping girls in school. The topic is only the vehicle. Whatever your group picks, you will use exactly the same collaboration skills to build it together.

You do not have to choose your own topic alone. You will agree it together with your group in a teacher session. For now, keep a note of any local problem that makes you curious or a little bit annoyed, because those feelings often point to a great shared Challenge.
bullets: Cutting down plastic waste in our school and market
Clean, safe water for every family
Keeping children, especially girls, in school
Road safety on busy streets
Saving energy, or using solar power
Protecting wildlife, such as sea turtles on the Berbera coast
Healthy food and better school meals

explainers.title: What is collaboration, really?
explainers.body:
Many people think teamwork just means being in the same room while everyone does their own thing. Real collaboration is more than that. Collaboration is a group of people agreeing on a shared goal, sharing the work fairly, and helping each other so that together they produce something better than any of them could alone.

Good collaboration usually moves through a cycle:

You will learn every step in this unit. Notice that collaboration is not simply about being nice. It is a set of skills you can practise and improve, exactly like research. Some very kind people struggle in teams because they avoid every disagreement, and some blunt people do well because they contribute clearly and listen. Collaboration is a skill, not a personality you are born with, which means anyone can get better at it. And like research, you already do it in everyday life without calling it a skill.

Nobody is a perfect teammate, and you will sometimes catch yourself in an unhelpful habit. That is fine. Noticing it is the first step to changing it, and this whole unit is your chance to practise.
bullets: Agree on a clear shared goal that everyone understands.
Work out each person's strengths and agree who does what, fairly.
Contribute useful ideas towards the goal.
Listen actively and build on each other's ideas.
Handle any disagreement respectfully and reach agreement.
Produce the shared outcome together.
Review honestly how well the team worked, and how you can do better next time.
Helpful teammates share ideas, listen to others, follow through on their tasks, encourage quieter members, and stay calm when they disagree.
Unhelpful habits include complaining without helping, disappearing when there is work to do, always needing to be in charge, and arguing just to win.

explainers.title: Keep a teamwork journal
explainers.body:
Before you meet the first skill, start a simple habit that strong teams use: keep a teamwork journal. This can be a notebook or a document where you record how your group works together as you go. Each time your team meets, write the date and jot down what your role was, what you contributed, any disagreement and how you sorted it out, and one thing you want to do better next time.

A teamwork journal matters for three reasons. It helps you see your own part honestly, which you will need for Reflection. It reminds the whole group what you agreed, so nothing gets forgotten between sessions. And it makes the final team review far easier, because the story of your teamwork is already written down. Keep your journal beside you as you work through this unit.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Knowing your strengths and agreeing roles fairly
explainers.body:
Every strong team starts by working out who is good at what, then dividing the tasks fairly. This is the heart of Cambridge objective 5.1: the team assigns roles and divides tasks fairly, considering each member's skills and the time available, and works together towards a shared outcome.

Fair does not mean everyone does exactly the same thing. It means the work is shared so that no one is overloaded and no one is left with nothing to do, and so that people can use their strengths while still stretching a little. To agree roles well, a team asks three questions:
bullets: What are our strengths? Who is good at organising, listening, being creative, presenting, meeting deadlines, or encouraging others?
What tasks does our shared outcome need? List every job that must be done.
How much time do we have? Match the size of each job to the time available before the deadline.

explainers.title: Skill 2: Contributing useful ideas to a shared outcome
explainers.body:
A team is only as good as the ideas its members bring. Cambridge objective 5.2 asks each team member to introduce useful ideas that help achieve the shared outcome. The key word is useful. A useful idea is not just any idea; it is one that is relevant to your goal and moves the team forward.

You do not have to be the loudest person to contribute well. In fact, talking a lot is not the same as helping. A quiet member who offers one sharp, relevant idea contributes more than someone who talks constantly but says little. To make your ideas useful, check them against your shared goal before you share them.

explainers.title: Skill 3: Active listening and building on others' ideas
explainers.body:
Collaboration is at least as much about listening as it is about talking. Active listening means showing the speaker that you have really heard them, not just waiting for your turn to speak. It is one of the most powerful team skills you can build, and it is what makes a group feel safe enough for everyone to share.

Active listening has a few simple moves:

That last move, building on an idea, is what turns a group of individuals into a real team. When you say 'Yes, and ...', you take someone's idea and add to it, so the idea grows and the person feels valued. This is also how you draw in quieter members and meet the part of objective 5.2 about encouraging others to participate.
bullets: Look at the speaker and do not interrupt while they are talking.
Show you heard them by briefly repeating their idea back: 'So you are saying we should ...'.
Ask a question to understand more, rather than jumping straight to your own point.
Build on the idea using words like 'Yes, and ...' instead of 'No, but ...'.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Disagreeing respectfully and reaching agreement
explainers.body:
Every real team disagrees sometimes, and that is not a bad sign. Disagreement can make an idea stronger, if it is handled well. The part of objective 5.2 about working positively to resolve conflict is not about never arguing; it is about arguing about the idea, kindly, and then reaching agreement together.

Three habits keep a disagreement healthy:

It also helps to have sentence starters ready, so that in the heat of the moment you can disagree without sounding rude. Phrases such as 'I see your point, and I wonder if ...' or 'What if we combined both ideas by ...' let you push back on an idea gently. You will find a full list of these in your Skills Toolkit.
bullets: Separate the idea from the person. You can disagree with an idea while still respecting the person who offered it.
Look for the compromise. Very often two different ideas can be combined into a better third idea that uses the best of both.
Try to see the other point of view, even one you do not agree with at first. Understanding why someone thinks something is the fastest way to agreement.

explainers.title: Skill 5: Giving and receiving helpful feedback
explainers.body:
Once your team has a draft of its shared outcome, feedback makes it better. Feedback is honest, kind advice about a piece of work, meant to help improve it. Learning to give feedback well, and to receive it without getting upset, is one of the most grown-up team skills you can develop.

A simple, fair way to give feedback is two stars and a wish: name two things that work well (the stars), then one thing that could be better (the wish). Three rules keep your feedback helpful:

Receiving feedback well is its own skill. When someone gives you feedback, listen without interrupting, thank them, resist the urge to defend your work, and then choose one thing to act on. Remember that feedback is about the work, not about you as a person.
bullets: Focus on the work, not the person. Say 'the poster has a lot of text', not 'you wrote too much'.
Be kind but honest. Kindness without honesty does not help the team improve; honesty without kindness just hurts.
Be specific and useful. Instead of 'make it better', say 'try using less text so the photo stands out'.

explainers.title: Skill 6: Reviewing how well the team worked together
explainers.body:
When the shared outcome is finished, a strong team does one more thing: it looks back honestly at how it worked together. This is where Collaboration meets Reflection. You review two things: how effective the team was as a whole, and how well you played your own part.

An honest team review asks questions like these:

The most important word here is honest. A review that says 'everything was perfect' teaches you nothing. A review that admits 'we talked over each other at the start' is far more useful, because it shows the team exactly what to do better next time. Reviewing your own role honestly is a strength, not a weakness.
bullets: Did we finish our shared outcome on time?
Did everyone contribute and feel listened to?
Did we share ideas and value each other's contributions?
How did we handle disagreements?
What did we do best, and what should we improve next time?

explainers.title: How collaboration links to the other five skills
explainers.body:
Collaboration does not stand alone. It pulls together every other Global Perspectives skill and makes each one stronger.

So the collaboration you practise now is not a separate box. It is the skill that lets a group of people combine all their other skills into something bigger than any of them could build alone.

You can see all six skills at work in our group at once. They researched plastic waste, analysed which change would help the most, evaluated the feedback another team gave them, reflected on how well they worked, and will soon communicate their poster to the whole school. Collaboration was the thread that tied every other skill together.
bullets: Research feeds your team, because a member who brings well-researched ideas is far more useful than one who guesses.
Analysis helps you break the shared task into parts and roles, so the work can be divided fairly.
Evaluation lets your team judge which idea is strongest and weigh the feedback you receive.
Reflection grows every time your team reviews honestly how it worked together.
Communication is how your team shares its shared outcome clearly, so all your teamwork actually reaches an audience.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the collaboration cycle
explainers.body: You have now met every collaboration skill in this unit. Here is how they fit into one smooth cycle you can use for any team task:
bullets: Agree a clear shared goal that everyone understands.
Work out your strengths and divide the roles fairly (objective 5.1).
Contribute useful, relevant ideas to the shared outcome (objective 5.2).
Listen actively and build on each other's ideas.
Disagree respectfully and reach agreement together (objective 5.2).
Produce the shared outcome, then improve it using feedback.
Review honestly how well the team worked, and set a target for next time.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Communication. Once your team can work together well, communication teaches you to share your shared outcome clearly and convincingly, so that all your teamwork actually changes how an audience thinks. Strong collaboration now will make strong communication much easier later. Well done for learning to build things with other people, which is one of the most valuable skills you will ever have.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is the vehicle, and the skill is the destination.
In this unit your group will work on a real topic such as plastic waste or clean water.
But the point is not the topic. The point is to become a person who can work well in any team, on anything, for the rest of your life.

bigIdeas.title: Collaborating across different viewpoints
lines: Global Perspectives is about working respectfully with people who see the world differently from you. A good team welcomes different views instead of fearing them.
When the group planned the day to show their campaign, some members came from Muslim families and some from Christian families.
They listened to each other and agreed on a time that respected both Friday prayers and Sunday worship, so everyone could take part.
Reaching a fair agreement across different beliefs and viewpoints, without pushing one side, is at the very heart of collaboration.

bigIdeas.title: Two stars and a wish
lines: Star 1: One thing the work does well.
Star 2: A second thing the work does well.
Wish: One specific thing that would make it better, such as: try using less text so the photo stands out.
Sentence starters you can use when you give feedback, so it stays kind and specific:

bigIdeas.title: Remember the split all the way through
lines: Your AI tutor is your practice ground: plan roles, rehearse listening, and try out ideas safely with it first.
Your teacher session is the real match: that is where the actual teamwork with your group happens.
Plan it with your tutor now, then carry it out with your group next.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 5 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Collaboration.
Ask it: In one or two sentences, why is being able to work well with other people such a useful skill in life?
Then say: In this unit, please be my planning and rehearsal partner. I will get ready with you, then do the real teamwork with my group in my teacher sessions.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you now think collaboration means.
Ask the tutor: Is my definition missing anything important?
Then tell it one habit of a helpful teammate you are already good at, and one you would like to get better at.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your shared Challenge idea and the strengths you think you bring to a team.
Ask it to help you list all the jobs a poster or presentation on your topic would need.
Then rehearse a fair split with the tutor. Afterwards, agree the real roles together with your group in your next teacher session.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your group's shared goal, then brainstorm five possible ideas with it.
Ask the tutor: Which of my ideas are most relevant to the goal, and which should I drop?
Rehearse how you will offer your best idea clearly. Then share it with your real group in your teacher session.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to role-play a teammate sharing an idea, while you practise active listening.
Practise repeating the idea back and then building on it with the words Yes, and.
Ask the tutor for feedback on your listening. Then use these same moves with your real group in your teacher session.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a disagreement your group might have, then ask it to argue the opposite side to you.
Practise staying calm, using a polite sentence starter, and offering a compromise that combines both ideas.
When a real disagreement comes up in your teacher session, use what you rehearsed to help your group reach agreement.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Show your AI tutor a description of your draft outcome and ask it to give you two stars and a wish.
Then practise receiving that wish calmly: thank it, and name one change you could make.
Rehearse giving kind, specific feedback too. Then swap real feedback with another group in your teacher session.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Talk through an honest self-review with your AI tutor: what did you contribute, and what will you do better next time?
Ask it to help you turn your honest thoughts into a fair, specific target.
Then complete the team review together with your group in your teacher session, and compare what you each noticed.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your top three characteristics and your reasons.
Ask it: Which of these ten habits build a team up, and which pull it down?
Then tell the tutor which helpful habit you already show, and which one you would like to grow this unit.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor two or three local problems you care about, from the list in the Lesson file or your own.
Ask it: Which of these would make a good shared group project, and why?
Rehearse how you will suggest your favourite to your group kindly, and how you will listen to theirs.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor which team skills you are strong at: organising, listening, being creative, presenting, meeting deadlines, or encouraging others.
Ask it to help you list every job your shared outcome will need.
Rehearse suggesting a fair split, and practise offering to take a job that fits your strength.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Remind your AI tutor of your shared goal, then brainstorm at least five ideas for your outcome with it.
Ask the tutor: Which of these ideas are most relevant to the goal, and which should I let go?
Rehearse explaining your best idea in one clear sentence.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to pretend to be a teammate and share an idea about your topic.
Practise the moves: do not interrupt, repeat the idea back, ask a question, then build on it with the words Yes, and.
Ask the tutor for feedback: did you really listen, or were you just waiting to talk?

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe a disagreement your group might have, then ask your AI tutor to argue the opposite side to you.
Practise a polite sentence starter, such as: I see your point, and I wonder if we could combine both ideas.
Keep going until you and the tutor reach a compromise that uses the best of both ideas.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your topic and draft five interview questions about it.
Ask it to check that your questions are clear and fair, and not leading.
Improve any weak question with the tutor's help.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what form your outcome will take and which part is your job.
Ask it to help you plan your part so it fits with the rest of the team's work.
Rehearse how you will present your part to the team.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe your draft outcome to your AI tutor and ask it for two stars and a wish.
Practise receiving the wish calmly: thank it, and name one change you will make.
Then rehearse giving kind, specific feedback, focusing on the work and not the person.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Give your AI tutor an honest self-review of your own role: what did you contribute, and what could you do better?
Ask it to help you turn one honest thought into a fair, specific target for next time.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three Challenge sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Based on our teamwork, what is one thing our group could do even better next time?
Ask the tutor to help you plan how you will raise that idea with your group kindly.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your rewritten feedback and your respectful sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your feedback is now kind, honest and focused on the work.
Ask the tutor to show you one more way to reword any line you found hard.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to tell you which answer showed the strongest teamwork thinking, and why.
Ask the tutor to give you one more team scenario like these to try.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your reflection answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how you grew as a teammate from the start of the unit to now.
Ask the tutor to suggest one collaboration habit to focus on in the next unit, and why.

speakingPrompts.title: A human touch
lines: Ask a family member which local problem they most wish the community would fix together.
Bring their answer, and your own ideas, to your next teacher session.
Your group can then compare everyone's ideas and agree on one shared Challenge together.

speakingPrompts.title: A real-world step
lines: With a trusted adult's help, ask your agreed questions to a few family members or neighbours.
Bring what you find back to your next teacher session so the team can use it in the shared outcome.

teacherSessions.title: Collaboration happens in everyday life too
lines: Imagine your family is preparing a big meal to welcome guests for a celebration.
You agree the shared goal: a good meal, ready on time. You share the work: one person shops, one cooks, one cleans, one welcomes the guests.
You listen to each other, you sort out the moment when two people both want the one pot, and you finish together.
That is real collaboration, and you already do it. This unit just helps you do it on purpose, with more skill.
Part of collaboration is knowing what a helpful teammate looks like. Some habits build a team up, and some pull it down.

teacherSessions.title: The group divides the plastic-waste roles fairly
lines: The team lists the jobs their poster and presentation will need: a plan, a design, some real interviews, a spokesperson, and photographs.
Nadia, who is organised, agrees to coordinate the plan and the deadlines. Sami, who is creative, will design the poster. Rohan, who is confident, will present.
Layla, a good listener, will interview neighbours about plastic use. That leaves Idris, so the team gives him a real and useful job: collecting photographs of blocked drains.
Every member has a fair share that fits their strength, and nobody is left out. That is objective 5.1 in action.

Notice one more thing the group did: they made sure Idris, their quietest member, had a real role, not a leftover one. A fair team shares the work so that everyone can contribute something they can be proud of.

teacherSessions.title: Sami contributes ideas, and the team weighs them
lines: Sami, who loves ideas, suggests three things for the plastic-waste poster: a big photo of a blocked drain, a cartoon turtle, and a long list of every kind of plastic.
The team keeps the photo of the drain, because it shows the local problem clearly and fits their goal.
They keep the turtle, because it links to the Berbera coast and catches the eye. They drop the long list, because it is not relevant and would crowd the poster.
Sami is not upset that one idea was dropped. Offering three ideas so the team can choose the best is exactly how a good member contributes.

See how the team judged each idea against the goal rather than against the person? Ideas are not good or bad because of who said them. They are useful or not useful depending on whether they help the shared outcome. Keeping that in mind makes it much easier both to offer ideas and to let some of them go.

teacherSessions.title: Layla listens Idris into the conversation
lines: The team is stuck for a strong message for the poster. Idris says quietly, almost to himself, maybe reusable cloth bags.
Layla notices. Instead of talking over him, she looks at him and repeats it back: so you are saying we should show people a reusable cloth bag they can use again and again.
Then she builds on it: yes, and we could show exactly where in the market they can buy one.
Idris, feeling heard, adds more: we could even work out how many plastic bags one cloth bag saves in a month. His quiet idea became the heart of the poster, because Layla listened.

teacherSessions.title: Nadia and Rohan disagree, then compromise
lines: Nadia wants a poster, because it is quick and the deadline is close. Rohan wants a video, because he thinks it would be more exciting.

Instead of arguing to win, Rohan says: I see why a poster is faster, and I still think moving pictures would grab people. Nadia replies: what if we make the poster now, and film a short clip later if we have time.
They combine both ideas. The poster meets the deadline, and the idea of a clip is saved for later.
Nobody lost. They separated the idea from the person, looked for a compromise, and reached agreement. That is objective 5.2 at its best.

teacherSessions.title: The group receives feedback and acts on it
lines: Another team, led by Yasmin and Grace, looks at the draft poster. Their two stars: the photo of the drain is powerful, and the message is clear.
Their wish: there is too much text, so the poster looks crowded and hard to read from far away.
Rohan feels a flash of wanting to argue, but instead the group thanks the other team and talks it over. Sami trims the words so the photo stands out.
The final poster is much stronger, all because the team received honest feedback without taking it personally.

teacherSessions.title: The group reviews its teamwork
lines: The team fills in a review grid together. They finished on time, everyone contributed, and they shared ideas well. Those are real strengths.
But Layla honestly notes that at the very start, two people kept talking over each other, and Idris almost did not get a word in.
So the team agrees on one thing to improve next time: let one person speak at a time, and check that the quietest member has been heard.
Each member also reviews their own role. Sami admits he sometimes pushed his ideas too hard; Nadia sees she could have shared the planning more.

teacherSessions.title: The group's whole journey, from problem to campaign
lines: Skill 1: They matched their strengths to roles and made sure even Idris had a real job.
Skill 2: Each member brought useful ideas, and the team kept the ones that fit the goal.
Skill 3: Layla listened Idris into the conversation, and his idea became the heart of the poster.
Skill 4: Nadia and Rohan disagreed about a poster or a video, then found a compromise.
Skill 5: They received honest feedback from another group and made their poster stronger.
Skill 6: They reviewed their teamwork honestly and agreed one clear thing to improve next time.

By following this cycle, an ordinary group of learners turned a worry about plastic in their streets into a real campaign they made together. In the Activities file, you will run the same cycle with your own group, planning each step with your AI tutor and carrying it out with real people.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Share your rankings with your team and compare them.
As a team, agree on the one characteristic you most want everyone to show.
Notice how your team reached agreement when your rankings were different.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Each member shares one topic idea and one reason they care about it.
As a team, agree on one shared Challenge. Notice how you reached agreement.
Write down your shared topic and one sentence on why your group chose it.

Agreeing a topic is your team's first taste of compromise. If two members wanted different topics, notice how you decided fairly, and whether the person whose idea was not chosen still feels part of the team. That feeling matters more than the topic itself.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: As a team, fill in a roles-and-responsibilities table (there is one in your Skills Toolkit).
For each member, write their strength, their role, their main task, and a deadline.
Check together: is the work shared fairly, and does everyone, including your quietest member, have a real job?
Write the finished roles into your teamwork journal, so no one forgets what they agreed to do.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Each member offers their best idea to the team. Nobody judges an idea by who said it.
As a team, decide which ideas fit the goal and belong in your outcome.
In your journal, note one idea you contributed and one idea from someone else that you helped improve.

Notice who found it easy to let an idea go, and who found it hard. Both feelings are completely normal. Letting go of your own idea for the good of the team is a real teamwork skill, and it gets easier every time you do it.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Run a short team discussion where each person must repeat the previous idea before adding their own.
Make a point of inviting your quietest member to speak, and build on what they say.
Afterwards, ask each other: did everyone feel listened to?

If someone felt talked over, that is useful to know rather than something to feel bad about. Agree one small change together, such as letting each person finish before the next person speaks, and try it in your next session.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: When a real disagreement comes up, use the sentence starters instead of arguing to win.
Look for a compromise that combines both ideas rather than choosing one winner.
In your journal, record what the disagreement was and how your team resolved it.

The goal of a disagreement is never to win, but to reach a decision the whole team can live with. A compromise that everyone accepts is far stronger than a victory that leaves one person feeling ignored, because that person still has to help build the outcome.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: As a team, share everyone's questions and agree on the best five to use.
Decide who will ask whom: family members, neighbours, shopkeepers or school staff.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Bring each person's part together into one draft outcome.
Check as a team: does every member's work fit the shared goal, and has everyone contributed?
Agree what still needs finishing before the next session.

Before you call the draft finished, check it against a simple list together: does it have a clear beginning, middle and end; a mix of words and images; text large enough to read; and content that answers your question with evidence? Fix anything missing as a team.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Swap your draft with another group and give each other two stars and a wish.
Receive their feedback without arguing; thank them and choose one thing to act on.
As a team, make one clear improvement based on the feedback you received.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Complete a team-review grid together (there is one in your Skills Toolkit).
Agree on one thing your team did best and one thing to improve next time.
Compare what each of you noticed. Being honest here is a strength, not a weakness.

Write your team's review into your teamwork journal. A team that reviews honestly, session after session, gets visibly better each time; a team that skips this step tends to keep repeating the same mistakes without noticing.

toolkit.title: The collaboration cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your task, good teamwork follows the same seven steps. Come back to this list whenever your team feels stuck.
items: Agree the goal: make sure everyone understands the shared outcome.
Share the roles: divide tasks fairly by strengths and time (objective 5.1).
Contribute ideas: offer useful, relevant ideas towards the goal (objective 5.2).
Listen and build: hear each other out and build on ideas with 'Yes, and ...'.
Resolve disagreement: argue about the idea, kindly, and reach agreement (objective 5.2).
Produce and improve: make the outcome, then improve it using feedback.
Review: look back honestly at how the team worked, and set a target.

toolkit.title: The Collaboration skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Collaboration is working with other people towards a shared goal, sharing the work fairly and helping each other, so that together you produce something better than any of you could alone. It is not just being in the same room. Real collaboration means agreeing a goal, dividing roles fairly, contributing useful ideas, listening and building on each other, handling disagreement with respect, and reviewing honestly how you worked.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, value every member, because a team is stronger when everyone, even the quietest person, contributes. Second, focus on the idea, not the person, whether you are choosing ideas, disagreeing, or giving feedback. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Cambridge Stage 7 Collaboration objectives
toolkit.intro: Global Perspectives sets out exactly what strong collaboration looks like at this stage. There are two Collaboration objectives, and every lesson in this unit works on them both. Here they are, restated simply. Your teacher may refer to these codes.

rows: The team assign roles and divide tasks fairly, considering the skills of team members and time available, and work together to achieve a shared outcome.
Work out who is good at what, share the jobs fairly, and pull together to make one shared outcome.
The team member introduces useful ideas to help achieve a shared outcome and works positively to resolve conflict, solve problems and encourage other team members to participate, when required.
Bring useful ideas, sort out disagreements kindly, help solve problems, and encourage others to join in.

toolkit.title: Helpful and unhelpful team habits
toolkit.intro: Every team is made of people, and people have habits. These ones build a team up or pull it down. Aim for the left column, and gently notice when you slip into the right.

rows: Always needs to be in charge

toolkit.title: Roles you might take in a team
toolkit.intro:
There is no single right set of roles, but most teams need these jobs covered. One person can hold more than one role, and a fair team makes sure every member, including the quietest, holds a real one.

When you agree roles, match each one to a real strength, but do not be afraid to stretch: a shy member might try presenting a small part, with the team's support.
items: Coordinator — keeps the plan, tracks who is doing what, and watches the deadline.
Ideas person — suggests new ways to do things and offers options to choose from.
Researcher — gathers the facts and the local views the outcome will need.
Maker or designer — builds the poster, slides or video.
Presenter — shares the finished outcome clearly with the audience.
Encourager — makes sure everyone is heard and draws in quieter members.

toolkit.title: Template: Roles and responsibilities
toolkit.intro: Copy this table and fill it in as a team. It makes objective 5.1 real: match each person's strength to a role, give them a clear task, and agree a deadline so the work is shared fairly.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for respectful disagreement
toolkit.intro: Use these to disagree about an idea without attacking the person. They keep a disagreement calm and point it towards agreement.
items: I see your point, and I wonder if ...
What if we combined both ideas by ...?
I understand why you think that. Could we also consider ...?
That could work. One thing I would add is ...
Help me understand your idea a bit more, then I will share mine.
Can we look for a middle way that uses the best of both?

toolkit.title: Giving and receiving feedback
toolkit.intro:
A simple, fair way to give feedback is two stars and a wish: two things that work well, then one thing that could be better. Always focus on the work, be kind but honest, and be specific.

When you receive feedback, use these four steps so it helps rather than stings:
items: Two things I really liked were ...
This part works well because ...
One thing that would make it even better is ...
Have you thought about trying ...?
I found this bit clear, and I wonder if the next part could ...
Listen without interrupting.
Thank the person for their help.
Do not rush to defend your work.
Choose one thing to act on, and change it.

toolkit.title: Template: Team review grid
toolkit.intro:
Copy this grid and complete it together when your outcome is finished. Answer honestly; an honest review is what makes the next project better.

Then finish two sentences together: 'We did best at ...' and 'Next time, we need to improve on ...'.

rows: We finished our shared outcome on time.
We listened to and valued each other's ideas.
We shared ideas and made space for quieter members.
We used feedback to improve our work.

toolkit.title: How to run a fair team discussion
toolkit.intro: When your team needs to make a decision, a little structure keeps things fair and calm and stops the loudest voice from deciding everything.
items: Agree what you are deciding, in one sentence, so everyone is talking about the same thing.
Go around the team so each person shares one idea before anyone argues.
Ask your quietest member for their view, by name and kindly.
Look for a compromise that combines the best of the ideas.
Check that everyone can live with the decision before you move on.

toolkit.title: What to do when teamwork gets hard
toolkit.intro: Every team hits a rough patch; it does not mean the team has failed. Here are common problems and quick fixes:
items: One person is doing everything. Stop and share the work again using the roles table.
A member has gone quiet. Invite them in by name and ask what they think.
Two people keep clashing. Focus on the idea, not the person, and look for a compromise.
The team is stuck on a decision. Give each idea one minute, then choose the one that best fits the goal.
Someone has not done their task. Ask kindly whether they need help, rather than blaming them.

toolkit.title: Signs your team is working well
toolkit.intro: Use this quick list to check the health of your team at any point in the project.
items: Everyone knows their role and what to do next.
Quieter members are speaking and being heard.
Disagreements are about ideas, not people.
Ideas are chosen because they fit the goal, not because of who said them.
The team is making steady progress towards the shared outcome.

checklists.title: Checklist: Am I listening actively?
checklists.intro: Tick each one during a team discussion. Active listening is how you make everyone, especially quieter members, feel able to share.
items: Look at the speaker and do not interrupt.
Repeat their idea back: 'So you are saying ...'.
Ask a question to understand more, before making your own point.
Build on the idea with 'Yes, and ...' rather than 'No, but ...'.
Invite a quieter member to share, by name and kindly.

challenge.intro: Your team needs one shared topic that matters where you live. Choosing it together is your first real act of collaboration. The best shared Challenge is one every member cares about a little, because you will all be working on it for the rest of the unit. Choosing it fairly, where everyone is heard and the final choice belongs to the whole team, sets the tone for everything that follows.
checkpoints: I was surprised to discover that ...
I used to think that working as a team was ...
Now I think that working as a team is ...

activities.title: What makes a good teammate?
activities.label: Activity 1: What makes a good teammate?
activities.intro:
Before you form your team, warm up by thinking about what a good teammate actually does. This helps you spot the habits you want in your group, and the habits in yourself you would like to grow. Imagine your team has been asked to organise a charity event for your school. Rank these ten characteristics from 1 (most important in a teammate) to 10 (least important):

There is no single correct order, but notice that some of these habits build a team up while others pull it down. Write your ranking, then write one sentence explaining your number one choice.
steps: Often disappears when there is work

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your top three characteristics and your reasons.
Ask it: Which of these ten habits build a team up, and which pull it down?
Then tell the tutor which helpful habit you already show, and which one you would like to grow this unit.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Share your rankings with your team and compare them.
As a team, agree on the one characteristic you most want everyone to show.
Notice how your team reached agreement when your rankings were different.

activities.title: Map your strengths and agree roles (objective 5.1)
activities.label: Activity 3: Map your strengths and agree roles (objective 5.1)
activities.intro: A fair team divides work by strengths and by the time available. This is objective 5.1 in practice. First work out your own strengths, then agree the roles together. Remember that fair does not mean identical: it means the load is shared, everyone can use a strength, and nobody, especially your quietest member, is left without a real job.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor which team skills you are strong at: organising, listening, being creative, presenting, meeting deadlines, or encouraging others.
Ask it to help you list every job your shared outcome will need.
Rehearse suggesting a fair split, and practise offering to take a job that fits your strength.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: As a team, fill in a roles-and-responsibilities table (there is one in your Skills Toolkit).
For each member, write their strength, their role, their main task, and a deadline.
Check together: is the work shared fairly, and does everyone, including your quietest member, have a real job?
Write the finished roles into your teamwork journal, so no one forgets what they agreed to do.

activities.title: Contribute useful ideas (objective 5.2)
activities.label: Activity 4: Contribute useful ideas (objective 5.2)
activities.intro: A useful idea is one that is relevant to your shared goal. This is objective 5.2 in practice. Practise generating ideas on your own, then choosing the best together. You are not trying to win; you are trying to give the team good options. Offering three ideas so the team can pick the strongest one is more useful than defending a single idea to the end.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Remind your AI tutor of your shared goal, then brainstorm at least five ideas for your outcome with it.
Ask the tutor: Which of these ideas are most relevant to the goal, and which should I let go?
Rehearse explaining your best idea in one clear sentence.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Each member offers their best idea to the team. Nobody judges an idea by who said it.
As a team, decide which ideas fit the goal and belong in your outcome.
In your journal, note one idea you contributed and one idea from someone else that you helped improve.

Notice who found it easy to let an idea go, and who found it hard. Both feelings are completely normal. Letting go of your own idea for the good of the team is a real teamwork skill, and it gets easier every time you do it.

activities.title: Practise active listening and building on ideas
activities.label: Activity 5: Practise active listening and building on ideas
activities.intro: Active listening means showing you truly heard someone, then building on their idea with 'Yes, and ...'. This is how you draw in quieter members and how a group of individuals becomes a real team. It is a skill you can rehearse safely with your AI tutor before you use it with real people.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to pretend to be a teammate and share an idea about your topic.
Practise the moves: do not interrupt, repeat the idea back, ask a question, then build on it with the words Yes, and.
Ask the tutor for feedback: did you really listen, or were you just waiting to talk?

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Run a short team discussion where each person must repeat the previous idea before adding their own.
Make a point of inviting your quietest member to speak, and build on what they say.
Afterwards, ask each other: did everyone feel listened to?

If someone felt talked over, that is useful to know rather than something to feel bad about. Agree one small change together, such as letting each person finish before the next person speaks, and try it in your next session.

activities.title: Rehearse resolving a disagreement (objective 5.2)
activities.label: Activity 6: Rehearse resolving a disagreement (objective 5.2)
activities.intro: Disagreement is normal and can make ideas stronger. The skill, and part of objective 5.2, is to argue about the idea, kindly, and reach agreement. This is the perfect thing to rehearse with your AI tutor, because it can play the person who disagrees with you without any of the real-life awkwardness. Practising the calm words now makes the real conversation much easier later.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe a disagreement your group might have, then ask your AI tutor to argue the opposite side to you.
Practise a polite sentence starter, such as: I see your point, and I wonder if we could combine both ideas.
Keep going until you and the tutor reach a compromise that uses the best of both ideas.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: When a real disagreement comes up, use the sentence starters instead of arguing to win.
Look for a compromise that combines both ideas rather than choosing one winner.
In your journal, record what the disagreement was and how your team resolved it.

The goal of a disagreement is never to win, but to reach a decision the whole team can live with. A compromise that everyone accepts is far stronger than a victory that leaves one person feeling ignored, because that person still has to help build the outcome.

activities.title: Gather local views together
activities.label: Activity 7: Gather local views together
activities.intro: A strong shared outcome uses real voices from your community, not just facts from a book. To develop a local perspective, you need information from local people: your family, neighbours, shopkeepers and school staff. A team in Mogadishu working on road safety might interview drivers and parents; your team will interview the people closest to your topic. Plan your questions with your tutor, then agree the best ones as a team and gather views together.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your topic and draft five interview questions about it.
Ask it to check that your questions are clear and fair, and not leading.
Improve any weak question with the tutor's help.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: As a team, share everyone's questions and agree on the best five to use.
Decide who will ask whom: family members, neighbours, shopkeepers or school staff.

boxes.title: A real-world step
lines: With a trusted adult's help, ask your agreed questions to a few family members or neighbours.
Bring what you find back to your next teacher session so the team can use it in the shared outcome.

activities.title: Build your shared outcome together
activities.label: Activity 8: Build your shared outcome together
activities.intro: Now your team turns all its work into one shared outcome: a poster, a presentation, or a short video. This is where objective 5.1 comes fully to life, because every member contributes the part that matches their role. A good shared outcome has a clear beginning, middle and end, uses a mix of words and images, and answers your question with evidence from your interviews.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what form your outcome will take and which part is your job.
Ask it to help you plan your part so it fits with the rest of the team's work.
Rehearse how you will present your part to the team.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Bring each person's part together into one draft outcome.
Check as a team: does every member's work fit the shared goal, and has everyone contributed?
Agree what still needs finishing before the next session.

Before you call the draft finished, check it against a simple list together: does it have a clear beginning, middle and end; a mix of words and images; text large enough to read; and content that answers your question with evidence? Fix anything missing as a team.

activities.title: Give and receive feedback
activities.label: Activity 9: Give and receive feedback
activities.intro: Feedback makes a draft better, but only if it is given kindly and received calmly. Practise giving two stars and a wish, and receiving a wish without getting defensive. Rehearsing with your AI tutor helps here, because it is easier to keep calm with a real person later once you have felt the words in practice.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe your draft outcome to your AI tutor and ask it for two stars and a wish.
Practise receiving the wish calmly: thank it, and name one change you will make.
Then rehearse giving kind, specific feedback, focusing on the work and not the person.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Swap your draft with another group and give each other two stars and a wish.
Receive their feedback without arguing; thank them and choose one thing to act on.
As a team, make one clear improvement based on the feedback you received.

activities.title: Review your teamwork
activities.label: Activity 10: Review your teamwork
activities.intro: When the outcome is finished, review honestly how your team worked. This is Collaboration meeting Reflection. A review that admits a weakness is far more useful than one that says everything was perfect, because it shows your team exactly what to do better next time.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Give your AI tutor an honest self-review of your own role: what did you contribute, and what could you do better?
Ask it to help you turn one honest thought into a fair, specific target for next time.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Complete a team-review grid together (there is one in your Skills Toolkit).
Agree on one thing your team did best and one thing to improve next time.
Compare what each of you noticed. Being honest here is a strength, not a weakness.

Write your team's review into your teamwork journal. A team that reviews honestly, session after session, gets visibly better each time; a team that skips this step tends to keep repeating the same mistakes without noticing.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Try every question before you look at the answer key, and give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does 'collaboration' mean?
practice.answer: Collaboration means working with others towards a shared goal, sharing the work fairly, so together you make something better than one person could alone. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: True or false: a good team is made of people who are all good at exactly the same things.
practice.answer: False. A strong team is made of different people whose strengths fit together.

practice.prompt: Cambridge objective 5.1 is about dividing roles and tasks how? (a) equally by size (b) fairly, by strengths and time (c) by who talks loudest.
practice.answer: (b) fairly, by strengths and time available.

practice.prompt: Name two strengths a team member might bring, such as organising or listening.
practice.answer: Any two of: organising, listening, being creative, presenting, meeting deadlines, encouraging others, following instructions, sharing ideas.

practice.prompt: A useful idea is one that is ______ to the shared goal.
practice.answer: Relevant.

practice.prompt: Active listening includes repeating an idea back and building on it. Which starter helps you build on an idea: 'No, but ...' or 'Yes, and ...'?
practice.answer: 'Yes, and ...'.

practice.prompt: When you disagree in a team, should you attack the person or the idea?
practice.answer: The idea, never the person.

practice.prompt: Two different ideas combined into a better third idea is called a ______.
practice.answer: A compromise.

practice.prompt: In the feedback method 'two stars and a wish', what is the wish?
practice.answer: The one thing that could be better (the area for improvement).

practice.prompt: True or false: when someone gives you feedback, you should defend your work straight away.
practice.answer: False. You should listen, thank them, and not defend your work straight away.

practice.prompt: Name one thing an honest team review should ask about.
practice.answer: Any one of: did we finish on time; did everyone contribute; were people listened to; how did we handle disagreement; what should we improve.

practice.prompt: In our model, who is your planning and rehearsal partner, and where does the real teamwork happen?
practice.answer: My AI tutor is my planning and rehearsal partner; the real teamwork happens with my group in my teacher sessions (and with family and community).

practice.prompt: Which of these is an unhelpful team habit: encouraging others, disappearing when there is work, or listening?
practice.answer: Disappearing when there is work to do.

practice.prompt: Give one reason why it helps to make space for your quietest team member to speak.
practice.answer: Any sensible reason, such as: quieter members often have good ideas; everyone deserves to be heard; the team gets more ideas to choose from.

practice.prompt: Name one thing that makes a shared outcome, such as a poster or presentation, effective for its audience.
practice.answer: Any one of: a clear structure with a beginning, middle and end; a mix of words and images; text big enough to read; content that answers the question; arguments supported with evidence.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each collaboration word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Collaboration
options: A. Something a team produces together, such as a poster or presentation.
B. Honest, kind advice about a piece of work, meant to help improve it.
C. Working with others towards a shared goal to make something better than one person could alone.
D. A disagreement between team members.
E. Showing a speaker you truly heard them, then building on their idea.
F. An agreement that combines the best of two different ideas.
practice.answer: C — Working with others towards a shared goal to make something better than one person could alone.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Shared outcome
practice.answer: A — Something a team produces together, such as a poster or presentation.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Compromise
practice.answer: F — An agreement that combines the best of two different ideas.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Active listening
practice.answer: E — Showing a speaker you truly heard them, then building on their idea.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Feedback
practice.answer: B — Honest, kind advice about a piece of work, meant to help improve it.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Conflict
practice.answer: D — A disagreement between team members.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Sami keeps offering ideas that do not fit the goal, and the team is running out of time. What could the team say to keep him contributing usefully?
practice.answer: Thank Sami for his energy, then gently ask the team to check each idea against the goal and the time left, so his ideas stay useful.

practice.prompt: Idris has a good idea but has not spoken all session. What is one thing Layla could do to bring him in?
practice.answer: Layla could look at Idris, invite him by name to share, repeat his idea back, and build on it so he feels heard.

practice.prompt: Nadia wants a poster and Rohan wants a video, and the deadline is close. Suggest a compromise that uses both ideas.
practice.answer: Make the poster now to meet the deadline, and film a short video clip later if there is time. Both ideas are used.

practice.prompt: Another group tells your team the poster has too much text. You feel like arguing. What should you do instead?
practice.answer: Do not argue. Thank the other group, talk it over as a team, and choose one change to make, such as cutting some text.

practice.prompt: Your team finished on time but two people talked over each other at the start. What honest target should the team set for next time?
practice.answer: A fair target such as: let one person speak at a time, and check that our quietest member has been heard.

practice.prompt: A team in Mogadishu cannot agree on who should present their work to the class. Suggest a fair way for them to decide.
practice.answer: Let each person say whether they want to present, then decide together based on who is comfortable, or share the presenting so more than one person has a part.

An early version of your outcome that you will improve.
What your team is trying to achieve together.
Feedback given to you by another learner or team.
A small, clear thing you aim to improve next time.

To give someone a reason to take part and try hard.

mistakes: Dividing work by who talks loudest instead of by strengths and time.
Leaving your quietest member with no real role.
Judging an idea by who said it rather than whether it fits the goal.
Arguing to win instead of looking for a compromise.
Giving feedback that attacks the person instead of the work.
Defending your work the moment you receive feedback.
Ending a project without an honest review of how the team worked.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what does 'collaboration' mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Collaboration means working with others towards a shared goal, sharing the work fairly, so together you make something better than one person could alone. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

questions.prompt: True or false: a good team is made of people who are all good at exactly the same things.
questions.modelAnswer: False. A strong team is made of different people whose strengths fit together.

questions.prompt: Cambridge objective 5.1 is about dividing roles and tasks how? (a) equally by size (b) fairly, by strengths and time (c) by who talks loudest.
questions.modelAnswer: (b) fairly, by strengths and time available.

questions.prompt: Name two strengths a team member might bring, such as organising or listening.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: organising, listening, being creative, presenting, meeting deadlines, encouraging others, following instructions, sharing ideas.

questions.prompt: A useful idea is one that is ______ to the shared goal.
Active listening includes repeating an idea back and building on it. Which starter helps you build on an idea: 'No, but ...' or 'Yes, and ...'?
When you disagree in a team, should you attack the person or the idea?
Two different ideas combined into a better third idea is called a ______.
In the feedback method 'two stars and a wish', what is the wish?
questions.modelAnswer: The one thing that could be better (the area for improvement).

questions.prompt: True or false: when someone gives you feedback, you should defend your work straight away.
questions.modelAnswer: False. You should listen, thank them, and not defend your work straight away.

questions.prompt: Name one thing an honest team review should ask about.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: did we finish on time; did everyone contribute; were people listened to; how did we handle disagreement; what should we improve.

questions.prompt: In our model, who is your planning and rehearsal partner, and where does the real teamwork happen?
questions.modelAnswer: My AI tutor is my planning and rehearsal partner; the real teamwork happens with my group in my teacher sessions (and with family and community).

selfAssessment.statement: I understand what the word 'collaboration' means.
I can name my own strengths as a team member.
I can help my team divide roles and tasks fairly (5.1).
I can contribute useful, relevant ideas to a shared outcome (5.2).
I can listen actively and build on other people's ideas.
I can encourage a quieter team member to take part.
I can disagree respectfully and help reach agreement (5.2).
I can give feedback that is kind, honest and about the work.
I can receive feedback without getting defensive.
I can review honestly how well my team worked together.
